column2: You will see slain by me, like two jewels threaded on a string, the two cousins, sons of father's sister and mother's brother, unconquered brothers.
In Arjuna, Gandiva; in Krishna, the discus; Garuda and the monkey standard—these terrify the timid and delight me, Shalya.
But you, ill-natured, foolish, unskilled in great battles, have descended to fear and in terror speak much unbound nonsense.
For some reason you praise those two, born in a bad country; I shall surely slay them in battle and then slay you with your kinsmen.
Evil-minded, born in a sinful land, stain of the lesser kshatriyas, being a friend yet a foe, why do you try to frighten me with the two Krishnas?
Either I shall slay those two today, or they me, standing in battle; I do not fear the two Krishnas, knowing my own strength.
A thousand Vasudevas or hundreds of Phalgunas I alone shall slay; be silent, man from a bad country.
Women, children, old men, and people at play mostly sing verses as if studying; hear from me, Shalya, those verses about the evil-minded Madrakas.
They were recited by Brahmanas in the king's presence as they should be; hearing them, fool, concentrate, and then either bear them or reply better.
The Madraka is ever a betrayer of friends; he who hates us is a Madraka. There is no friendship in a Madraka, a base-spoken, lowest of men.
The Madraka is ever evil-souled, always untruthful and crooked; we have heard that wickedness among the Madrakas extends to the end.
Father, mother, son, mother-in-law, father-in-law, maternal uncles, son-in-law, daughter, brother, grandson and kinsmen, all of them,
friends, guests, and slaves, male and female, are mingled together; women mixed with men, known and unknown, as they please.
In whose houses the remaining people, always eating barley-gruel, drinking liquor, with beef and meat, dance and laugh.
And what things go on unbound and by wish, with people talking at will among themselves, how could there be dharma in those?
Among the destroyed Madrakas, known for inauspicious deeds, one should practise neither enmity nor friendship.
There is no association with a Madraka, for the Madraka is fickle; among the Madrakas and the Gandharakas purity is hard to touch.
By a priest who sacrifices for kings, the oblation given is lost.
As a Brahmana who performs rites for shudras goes to disgrace, so those who hate Brahmanas always come to disgrace here.
There is no association with a Madraka; poison struck by a scorpion is neutralised; by an Atharvan mantra complete remedy is made.
So the wise make a cure for one bitten by a scorpion and struck by various poisons, and that is seen to be true. Knowing this, be silent, and hear my further word.
Women who, bewildered by liquor, dance having cast off their clothes, uncontrolled in union, roaming as they please—how can the son of such, a Madraka, speak of dharma?
Those who stand and relieve themselves like a she-camel at a bridle, those shameless ones, their modesty lost, here and there—you, the son of such, wish to speak of dharma here.
When Suviraka is begged for, the Madraka woman, not wishing to give, utters this harsh speech, striking her thighs:
Let no one beg me for Suviraka, which is dear to me; I would give a son in return, but I would not give Suviraka.
We have heard that the Madraka women are tall, shameless, wrapped in blankets, gluttonous and mostly lacking purity.
Such and much more could be said by me or others, from the tip of the hair to the tip of the nail, of those who are to be spoken of, who are on evil paths.
How could the Madrakas, Sindhus and Sauviras know dharma here—they born in a sinful land, Mlecchas, unskilled in dharmas?
We have heard that this is the foremost dharma of a kshatriya: to lie slain in battle, honoured by the good.
If I were to be released from the clash of weapons, that would not be my first choice, wishing for heaven at death.
I am a dear friend of the wise son of Dhritarashtra; for him are my life and whatever wealth I have.
Clearly you too have been planted by the Pandavas, born in a sinful land; for you behave towards us in everything as an enemy.
Indeed I cannot be turned from battle even by hundreds like you, as a knower of dharma cannot be by atheists.
Lament and wither as you like, like a deer tormented by heat; I cannot be frightened, standing in a kshatriya's way of life.
Remember the course told to me earlier by my teacher Rama, for the lions among men who give up their bodies and never retreat in battles.
Know me to be ready to protect my own and to slay the foe, and following the supreme conduct of Pururavas.
I see no being in the three worlds, Madraka, who could turn me from this purpose; that is my opinion.
Knowing this, be silent; why do you speak so much through fear? I will not kill you and give you to the flesh-eaters, lowest of the Madrakas.
Shalya, you live by these three: waiting on friends, regard for Dhritarashtra's son, and patient endurance of blame.
If you speak such words again, king of the Madras, I shall fell your head with a mace like a thunderbolt.
Man from a bad country, today either you will hear, or see, that the two Krishnas slay Karna, or Karna slays them."
Having said this, Radheya, O lord of men, again said to the king of the Madras, calmly, "Go, go."
[Shalya said:] "Just as you are not intoxicated by drink, nor is it the same, so I cure you in friendship while you are heedless.
Hear from me, Karna, this crow-parable that is told; having heard it, do as you please, lowest of your family.
I do not remember any sin in myself, Karna, for which you, mighty-armed, wish to kill me who am blameless.
But I must speak, if it is good for you, to be understood—especially as one in the chariot and well-wisher of the king.
Level and uneven ground, the strength and weakness of the chariot-warrior, the fatigue and weariness of the horses along with the warrior,
knowledge of the weapon, the cries of beasts and birds, burden and overburden, and treatment of arrows,
use of weapons, fighting and omens—all this must be known by me as head of the household of this chariot. Therefore, Karna, I tell you this illustration.
There was a vaishya at the edge of the sea, rich in wealth and grain, a sacrificer, giver of gifts, patient, pure, devoted to his own duty.
Many sons, dear children, kind to all beings, he dwelt fearless in the realm of a king devoted to dharma.
A crow fed on the leavings of his many young, renowned sons.
The vaishya's boys always gave him meat and rice, curd, milk, sweet rice, honey and ghee.
Fed on leavings by the vaishya's boys, that crow, proud, despised birds equal to him and better.
Then once swans, with gold-marked wings, joyful, flying like Garuda, came by the sea's edge.
The boys, seeing the swans, said to the crow, "You are the most distinguished of birds, O flier."
Cajoled by those small-minded boys, the bird, through folly and pride, took their words to be true.
Desiring to test them, he flew at them, "Who among these is best?"—proud of leavings, the crow, among many that fly far.
Whom he regarded as the foremost of those far-flying swans, to that bird the ill-minded one called out: "Let us fly!"
Hearing that, the swans who were assembled there laughed at the crow's much talk, the strong ones, best of flyers, and those gold-winged birds said to the crow:

We are swans, roaming this earth, dwellers at Manasa, and we are ever honoured among birds for our long flight.
mahabharata:8:28.21	How, ill-minded one, being a crow, do you challenge to a flying contest a strong swan of mighty frame and long flight? How, crow, do you speak of flying with us?
Then the foolish crow, reviling the swan's words again and again, replied, boasting from lightness of birth:

I have flown a hundred and one flights, no doubt; each flight of a hundred yojanas, variegated and of various kinds:
mahabharata:8:28.24	flying up, flying down, flying forward, flying out, flying in, flying together, flying crosswise and flying beyond,
mahabharata:8:28.25	flying apart, flying around, flying forth, good flying, over-flying, great flying, flying in and flying around,
mahabharata:8:28.26	going and coming, returning, and many circling flights; I shall perform them before your eyes today, and then you will see my strength.
When the crow had spoken thus, one swan, laughing, replied to the crow; hear those words from me.

You, crow, have flown a hundred and one flights, surely; but all birds know only one flight.
mahabharata:8:28.29	I, crow, know no other; fly then, red-eyed one, in whatever way you think.
Then the crows who were assembled there laughed: "How could a swan surpass a hundred flights with one flight?
With a single flight he will outdo one of a hundred—the swan's flight; the crow is strong and of swift valour."
Then the swan and the crow set off in rivalry; the gold-winged swan with one flight, the crow with a hundred.
The swan flew and the crow flew, the crow wishing to astonish by his flights, proclaiming his own deeds.
Then seeing the crow's variegated and other flights, the crows, delighted, shouted with those cries.
They mocked the swans and said unpleasant things, and flying up and up, they said "Just a moment!" again and again.
They fell from treetops and from the ground and flew up again, making many kinds of cries, then hoping for victory.
The swan began to fly gently only and fell behind the crow for a moment, O revered one.
Slighting the swans' speed, the crow said, "The swan that flew up has fallen behind."
Hearing that, the swan flew towards the western quarter, over and over at speed, towards the sea, Varuna's abode.
Then fear entered the crow, bewildered, seeing no island or tree, falling weary: "Where shall I alight, tired, in this ocean of water?"
For the sea is unbearable, home of many hosts of creatures, shining with hundreds of great beings, surpassing even the sky.

Because of the depth of the sea there is no distinction, lowest of your family, among quarters, sky and water; the sea is hard to conquer, Karna—for the water's long fall, what then for a crow, Karna?
Then the gold-winged swan, flying beyond for a moment, looking at the crow, "just a moment," could not turn back, and having gone ahead, looked back at the crow.
Seeing him thus falling behind, the swan said this, wishing to raise him as he sank, remembering the vow of the good.

You who told of many flights again and again—fly, and do not utter what you will not tell us.
mahabharata:8:28.46	What flight is this called, crow, that you are doing now? You touch the water with your wings and again and again with your beak.
The crow, touching the water of the ocean with wings and beak, distressed and very weary, suddenly fell.
[The swan said:] "The hundred and one flights you spoke of, crow, the various ones, were false, as is clear today."
[The crow said:] "Proud of leavings, swan, I thought myself like Garuda, and I scorned many crows and other birds. I take refuge in you with my life, swan; take me to an island.
If I reach my own country safe again, swan, I will not slight anyone; deliver me from this calamity."
Saying this, wretched, lamenting, senseless, crying "Crow! Crow!", sinking in the great ocean,
the swan, coming up, lifted the crow, drenched with water and terrible to see, with his feet, trembling, and slowly placed him on his back.
Having placed the senseless crow on his back, Karna, the swan came again to the island from where they had flown in rivalry.
Setting him down there and consoling that sky-ranger, the swan went off to the country he wished, swift as thought.
As that crow was in the vaishya's family fed on leavings, so you, fed on Dhritarashtra's sons' leavings, no doubt, despise all, even equals and betters, Karna.
Guarded by Drona, Drona's son, Kripa, Bhishma and the other Kauravas, why did you not then kill Partha, alone, in Virata's city?
When all of you, scattered and conquered by Kiritin like jackals by a lion, where was your valour then?
Seeing your brother slain and yourself conquered by Savyasachin, in the sight of the Kuru heroes you were the first to flee.
Likewise, Karna, in the Dvaita forest, attacked by gandharvas, leaving all the Kurus, you were the first to flee.
Having slain and conquered the gandharvas led by Chitrasena in battle, Partha released Karna and Duryodhana together with their wives.
Again the ancient power of Partha and of Keshava was recounted by Rama in the assembly, in the royal council, Karna.
You constantly heard that statement of Drona and Bhishma, who said the two Krishnas were unslayable, in the presence of kings.
How much shall I say there, by which Dhananjaya is superior to you as a Brahmana is to all beings.
Even now you will see, in the encounter, the son of Vasudeva and the Pandava Dhananjaya standing in their chariot.
Those two bulls among men, renowned among gods, asuras and men, famed for their splendour—you are like a glow-worm among men.
Knowing this, do not despise Achyuta and Arjuna, charioteer's son; those two lions among men—be silent, boaster, you who are as a horse to a man."
[Karna said:] "Shauri driving Arjuna's chariot, the Pandava's strength and great weapons—I know them as they are today, Shalya; that is hidden from you.
Yet I shall fight those two unassailable ones, the best of weapon-bearers, free of fear; but the curse of Rama and of the best of Brahmanas torments me more.
Long ago I lived with Rama under the guise of a Brahmana, wishing to obtain a divine weapon; even there, Shalya, Indra, wishing Phalguna's good, set an obstacle for me.
Having come to my thigh and entered it in the form of an ugly insect, a break was made; and from fear of my teacher I did not move; that Brahmana saw it.
Asked, I told that great sage, 'I am a charioteer's son'; he cursed me: 'This weapon gained by you through the pretext of being a Suta will not appear to you at the time of action,
except at the time of your death, since Brahman is not firmly in a non-Brahmana.' Today, in this tumultuous and terrible battle, dear one, that weapon is sufficient.
The swift, immeasurable lord of waters, who would drown the masses of beings, makes the sea a great serpent—only the shore restrains the immeasurable one.
Releasing masses of unerring arrows that pierce vital parts, feathered, hero-slaying, I will fight the son of Kunti in battle, the best of all bowstring-drawers in the world today.

Thus with strength I shall withstand the very strong one of great weapons, like the sea, hard to reach, fierce, with floods of arrows, drowning kings; like the shore I shall withstand Partha with arrows.
Today in battle, equal to whom I deem no other man taking up a bow—he who could conquer gods and asuras in battle—see with him my most dreadful fight today.
The overproud Pandava, eager for battle, will come against me with superhuman great weapons; meeting his weapon with weapons in battle, I shall fell Partha with the best of arrows.
Blazing even like the sun, with fully attained rays, shining with fame, dispelling darkness, I shall cover Dhananjaya with arrows like a cloud above the sun.
As a cloud with showers extinguishes the fire Vaishvanara, with smoking flame, blazing, glorious, burning this world, so I shall quench Partha in battle with showers of arrows.
The crusher, the strong, the striker, the breaker, the fierce wind—I shall withstand in battle the enraged and unforgiving Dhananjaya, like the Himalaya.
The skilled one, unattached on chariot paths, ever bearing the yoke in wars, foremost hero, best of all archers in the world, I shall withstand Dhananjaya in battle.
Today in battle, equal to whom I regard no other man among men taking a bow, who could bear this whole earth—knowing so, I am about to fight him.
He who at Khandava defeated all beings with the gods—what other man, to save his life, would wish to fight him but me?
I could tell with joy the manliness of that Pandava in the assembly of kshatriyas; why, fool, did you, speaking foolishly with a confused mind, tell me Arjuna's manliness?
The disagreeable, harsh, cruel, mean, reviling, who is intolerant of the tolerant—I could slay hundreds of such; I forgive you by forbearance because of the course of time.

You spoke disagreeable things on behalf of the Pandavas, attacking me like a fool, evil-doer; you who are crooked towards my straightness are slain—a betrayer of a friend; friendship is made by seven steps.
This is the time of death, most dreadful, that Duryodhana has come to battle; wishing the success of his purpose I shall go against them, where there is no certainty.
'Friend' is derived from the roots mid, nand, pri, trai, mud, as taught earlier by the learned; and all that I have in Duryodhana.
'Enemy' (shatru) from shad, shas, shay, shri, shvi and sometimes from prefixes in many ways, and from su-d; mostly all that is in you, and that is in me.
For Duryodhana's sake and for your displeasure, for fame's sake, for my own and for my lord's, I shall therefore fight the Pandava and Vasudeva with effort; see that deed of mine today.
See my supreme weapons today, Brahma weapons, divine and human; I shall attack the fierce-valoured one like a rutting elephant a rutting elephant.
I shall loose the Brahma weapon, unconquerable by mind, incomparable, for Partha's defeat; and even by it he would not be freed in battle, unless my wheel falls in a pit today.
Not from Vaivasvata with the rod in hand, nor from Varuna with the noose, nor from the lord of wealth with his mace, nor from Vasava with his thunderbolt,
nor from anyone else do I fear an aggressor; know, Shalya, that I am fearless.
Therefore I have no fear of the Parthas nor of Janardana; today there will be a fight between those two and me.
A Brahmana told me, 'Your wheel will fall into a pit'; for one fighting in battle, danger comes in a narrow place.
Therefore I fear greatly the Brahmana's word; for those are lords of the moon-kings, rulers of pleasure and pain.
Careless, I once struck with an arrow the calf of a sacrificial cow of that treasure of austerity, a Brahmana, as it wandered in the lonely place, Shalya.
Though I offered seven hundred plough-pole-tusked elephants and hundreds of servants, he did not show me grace.
Though I brought fourteen thousand black cows with white calves, I did not obtain grace from that best of the twice-born.
I offered him honour and all my house rich with every desire and whatever wealth I had; he did not accept.
Then he said to me, who begged earnestly for pardon: 'Charioteer, what I have said will be so; it will not be otherwise.
He who speaks untruth would destroy creatures and so incur sin; therefore, to protect dharma, I do not venture to speak falsely.
Do not harm the Brahmanic course; you have made atonement. No one in the world would make my word untrue; accept it.'
This I have told you, though provoked, out of friendship; I know you are insulting me; be silent and hear my reply."
[Karna said:] "What you said to me by way of illustration, Shalya, I cannot be frightened by words in battle.
If all the gods with Vasava were to fight me, I would still have no fear; how much less from Partha with Keshava?
I cannot be frightened by mere words in any way; know another whom you can frighten in battle.
This much is the strength of a low man: the harshness with which you speak to me; unable to attain our qualities, you babble much, ill-minded one.
Karna, O revered one, was not born here to be afraid; I was born for valour and likewise for fame.
Listen with attention, lord of the Madras, to what I heard being said in Dhritarashtra's presence.
Brahmanas used to attend Dhritarashtra, telling of the many wondrous countries and of kings of former times.
There an aged best of the twice-born, reviling the Bahlika country and the Madras, spoke words of past tales.
Those who are shut out by the Himalaya, scorned by the Ganga, Sarasvati, Yamuna and Kurukshetra,
those who live between the five rivers with the Sindhu as sixth, outside dharma and impure—the Bahlikas—should be avoided.
The banyan named Govardhana, the crossroad named Subhandaka—this is the gate of the royal house; I have remembered it since boyhood.
I lived among the Bahlikas on very pressing business; therefore their conduct became known to me by residence.
The city named Shakala, the river named Apaga, the Jartikas—the Bahlikas' ways are much condemned.
Drinking grain-spirit and Gauda liquor, eating beef with garlic, cakes and meat, they are lacking in character.
They laugh, sing and dance, drunk, with women, unclothed, outside the city houses and walls, garlanded and anointed.
With various drunken songs like the braying of asses and camels, drunk with excess, they talk to one another.
They cry "Alas, alas!" and "He has killed her husband!" and dance, dull and unrestrained on festival days.
Living in Kurujangala among those arrogant ones, one of the Bahlika chiefs, not very glad at heart, sang:

Surely she, tall and fair, clad in fine blanket, lies remembering me, the Bahlika living among the Kurus.

mahabharata:8:30.25	becoming strong on the roads, when shall we, trampling the path, go on beating and offering the tribute of the wicked?
When that mighty archer was slain, the three surviving chariot-warriors in the night, in fury, O king of kings, slew the Panchala soldiers.
How shall I be able to hear Bhima's words, Sanjaya, by whom my full hundred sons were slain, single-handed?
What Krishna said to me in the midst of the assembly for my good—'Enough of enmity, king; let your son be reconciled'—
But this great sorrow ever dwells in my heart, having caused this great destruction of kinsmen, brought about by greed.
And he said to her, "This is the lowest serpent, the killer of your son; tell quickly, noble lady, for what reason he should be killed."
If you wish welfare for your family and yourself, king, let this evil-souled, foolish king Suyodhana be put to death.
Through Vidura's influence, even his weighty tasks were accomplished with very light means from the neighbouring lords.
They, placing Samba in front, adorned like a woman, approached and said, afflicted by the rod of fate:
Hearing his words, the townspeople and country people, greatly troubled in mind, did not welcome those words.
He has attained this place by kshatriya duty, he who was fearless in great danger, the lord of the earth.
